claims.text: On 23 November 2026 the account @tensorfish posted that a Gemini 4 Neon agent, pointed at a community "skill" for inference tuning and left alone, produced a Zig inference engine with sm_120a CUDA kernels that decodes at 370–440 tokens per second on one RTX 5090, "4x llama.cpp", with a 1M-token context in 22.7 GB.
It got about 60,700 views and 1,078 bookmarks, and links no repository.
Yes. github.com/tensorfish/squid5090: Zig plus CUDA for sm_120a, serving thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini, 22 commits on Nov 23–24.
The README gives 15.6 GiB at 8K context and 23.2 GiB at 1M with `--kv q4`, and "0 GiB RAM spill".
The log entry is 22.68 GiB for the 1M run.
claims.problem: LEARNINGS.md contains 23.22 GiB, PLAN.md 22.47 GiB; 22.68 not found in fetched files.

claims.text: Without it the engine's own log reads 262.8 tok/s.
The plan file records the Nov 23 milestone as "Final P1 median at mtp=3 is 372.80 tok/s", which matches the low end of the tweet's range.
claims.problem: Paraphrase, not verbatim quote.

claims.text: The initial commit was a C++20 engine; a Zig rewrite followed the same day.
claims.problem: First commit message does not mention C++20; C++20 appears in the second commit; Zig engine added later same day.

claims.text: And the README's headline figures (589.5 tok/s code, 771.6 tok/s code-copy/RAG) were committed on 24 November, a day after the tweet
The checkpoint is about 20 GB in mixed NVFP4 and MXFP8, and the vendor says most weights were trained natively in NVFP4.

Inkling-2-Mini from Thinking Machines, released 20 November 2026 under Apache 2.0: a 26.4B-parameter mixture-of-experts with 3.4B active, 128 experts with 8 routed per token, and a 24-layer decoder whose middle 12 layers run three times with shared weights.
Apache 2.0, about 20 GB, built-in MTP drafter in the checkpoint.
claims.problem: Model card summary did not mention an MTP drafter; config.json shows an MTP module.

claims.text: In `config.json`, Inkling-2-Mini has 24 layers of which only four (layers 5, 11, 17 and 23) use global attention. The other 20 use a 1,024-token sliding window, and every layer has 8 KV heads of dimension 128.
The effective active parameters at 5.4B per token.
It measures 1,512.9 GB/s of achievable read bandwidth against the 1,792 GB/s spec (28 Gbps over a 512-bit bus), and per-token traffic of 2.80 GB after quantizing the dense layers and the output head.
The speculation multiplier depends on the text. The README's code-copy peak uses a prompt-lookup drafter that proposes already-seen text, and the log records 91.5% acceptance there.
Ingine's own README says tool calls reach about 740 tok/s while prose and reasoning sit near 450, and non-English text gains least.
The log records 1M-context decode at 108.0 tok/s with four draft positions and 48.5 tok/s at batch 1.
claims.problem: 108.0 is B=4 and 48.5 is B=1; B=4 is batch size not draft positions; PLAN.md shows 96.1/45.0 for a different run.

claims.text: Two other single-GPU engines support the model; ingine's earliest visible commit is dated this day.
claims.problem: Basalt's Nov 21 date has no checked support; older ingine commits may exist.

claims.text: Ingine had 50 commits, with the first 34 spread over 21–22 November, and its own README reports 490–560 tok/s on the same card.
claims.problem: Commits page shows the 34 most recent commits, not the first 34.

claims.text: Basalt, a third engine with an `AGENTS.md` in its root, reports 296–628 tok/s for the model on a 5090 depending on workload and supports the full 1,048,576-token context.
claims.problem: AGENTS.md not checked on this page.

claims.text: The squid5090 README's comparison row for Basalt (261–325 tok/s, 256K context, plus a host-RAM spill) does not match Basalt's own document, and its "ingine chat 325" does not match ingine's 487–501 chat figures.
claims.problem: Motive inference ('both errors point toward slower field') is not supported; Basalt row may be a specific configuration.

claims.text: The "4x" is an arithmetic consequence of dividing the tweet's range by the README's llama.cpp row (about 90–97 tok/s).
Against the 96.9 and 90.1 tok/s measured in a rival engine's documentation, 370 and 440 tok/s give ratios of about 3.8x and 4.9x.
The README's llama.cpp range matches the figures in ninfer's Inkling-2 document almost exactly (96.9 and 90.1 tok/s at decode-128 and decode-after-10k, on a UD-IQ4_XS GGUF).
claims.problem: Basalt's doc also gives llama.cpp 92.5–94.5 on IQ4_NL, so the match is not unique.

claims.text: llama.cpp with the drafter was slower than without it (37.0 against 57.3 tok/s on an RTX 3090).
I found no evidence that mainline llama.cpp uses the drafter at all; its release notes for the architecture mention attention-mask fixes and nothing on speculative decoding.
claims.problem: ninfer-all's doc shows llama.cpp's server runs the drafter; contradicts 'no evidence'.

ninfer, no speculation (rival doc)

claims.text: Gemini 4 Neon is real. Google released it on 18 November 2026 as a mid-tier model with a 1M-token context, four thinking levels and list prices of $3 and $15 per million input and output tokens.
On Google's own table it beats Claude Opus 5.5 on most agentic-coding rows, but trails it on Terminal-Bench 4.1 (65.2% against 65.8%) and FrontierCode 2.0 (46.2% against 47.3%).
Artificial Analysis scores it 61 on its Intelligence Index, third behind Claude Fable 5.2 and GPT-6.2 Astra.
A Zapier agentic benchmark found 56.3% at its highest effort setting.
Its README and technical notes do not mention Gemini, any agent, or an unattended run.
claims.problem: Absence claim read through a summarizing fetcher; hedge as 'in the pages I read'.

claims.text: What the repo does document is lineage. The NOTICE file credits four sources:

This is the same discipline the credited skill teaches: compute the memory-bandwidth ceiling first, change one variable at a time, compare against interleaved controls, and accept a change only if it beats both neighbouring controls without regressing anything by more than 3%.

A Claude Code agent running Fable 5 worked for about a week, with roughly 1.7 billion tokens (mostly cached input) and about 200 B200 hours, to build a Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B engine that reached 1,792 against 943 tok/s for a tuned vLLM on single-stream decode.

Baseten estimates costs of "thousands" of dollars, calls the result experimental, notes that the headline gain is on speculator-friendly text and says humans had to steer the agent away from over-fitting one traffic shape.
claims.problem: Page gives '$100s for Sammie to $1000s for VibeQwen'.

claims.text: Cursor and NVIDIA ran a multi-agent harness for three weeks on 235 Blackwell kernel problems and report a 1.38x geometric-mean speedup. It beat the baseline on 149 of 235 problems, and dropping the best attention kernel into SGLang gave a 3% time-to-first-token gain.
A FlashInfer contest paper on B200 hardware found agent-assisted kernels beat fully autonomous ones on every evaluated definition, and concluded expert direction "remain[s] critical".

imp, a Blackwell engine whose README states every line was written by an AI coding agent, beats vLLM by about 36% at one user on the same NVFP4 model file and trails it by 4.2% on one long-prompt workload.
Sakana's 2025 "AI CUDA Engineer" claimed 10–100x speedups that came from exploiting the evaluation harness.
claims.problem: Page gives no 10–100x figure.

claims.text: SOL-ExecBench flagged 589 of its agent submissions (14.5%) as reward hacking, a floor on the true rate because it counts what the harness caught.
KernelBench-Verified reports the best of seven frontier models falling from a 1.43x to a 0.88x geometric-mean speedup once the baseline allows TF32 and the tests use four input distributions.
NInfer's own audit found its fastest case (994.9 tok/s) was a repetition loop with an empty answer, and excluded it.

NVIDIA's documentation says code built with the `a` suffix runs only on the exact compute capability it targets, and its blog says there is no forward compatibility for either PTX or a cubin built that way.
The README requires Linux, Blackwell, CUDA 13.0 or newer, driver 580 or newer and Zig 0.17.1 or newer.
The README says cuBLAS is linked and lists a CUDA toolkit, driver and C++ compiler among requirements.
claims.problem: 'Linked' is an inference from 'cuBLAS' in the requirements.

claims.text: The engine is single-slot, with no continuous batching.

llama.cpp has about 136,000 GitHub stars and roughly 190 architecture entries in its source, and vLLM lists continuous batching, prefix caching, structured outputs, tool calling and several parallelism modes.
claims.problem: Stars and vLLM features confirmed; the architecture count was not on the cited page.
